extracted.intended_audience: War Department officials, military administrators, and government attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Compilation of legal principles and administrative rules governing the Secretary of War, Department of the Army, and employment of the Army (e.g., aid to civil authority, property, delegation, printing, counsel). Used to determine lawful scope of departmental actions and duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts of department heads are acts of the President
rubrics_metrics.description: All acts done and directions emanating from the heads of the executive departments in the course of their administrative duties are in law the acts and directions of the President, and are to be regarded as orders of the President whether or not so referred to therein.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include orders convening courts-martial, approving sentences, dismissing officers, establishing military reservations, promulgating army regulations. Cited authorities: multiple opinions (R. 5, 319, Nov. 1863; others).

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality of departmental decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: A decision upon a claim once arrived at by the head of a department is final and cannot be reopened by a successor except for new evidence, error of calculation, or fraud (or statutory authority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘New evidence’ must be evidence as to merits; mere reargument or citation of authorities is not new evidence. Reopening requires fraud, manifest error on face of proceedings, or newly discovered evidence presented within a reasonable time. (Citations: P. 58, 110, Feb. 1893; other opinions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may execute delegated ministerial acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where Congress authorizes the President to dispose of certain lands but does not in terms require execution, the execution of deeds may be a ministerial act that can legally be executed by the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held that execution of deeds under such statutes may be performed by Secretary (P. 48, 420, Aug. 1891).

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary/Commander-in-Chief limitations on property exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: The commander in chief (and by extension the Secretary) has no authority to exchange old public property for new property absent authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held no authority to exchange old for new property. (C. 2127, Mar. 14, 1896.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary cannot appropriate or stop officer's private pay or satisfy civil judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War is without authority to appropriate or stop an officer's pay for the use of his family, or to satisfy a judgment or decree of a civil court growing out of a private obligation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secretary may, however, bring officer to trial by court-martial for dishonorable conduct. Examples and citations: C. 3500 (Sept. 1897); C. 3819, 5482, 6882.

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department will not act as collector of private debts
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not within the War Department’s province to protect officers against suits by civilians claiming to be their creditors or to act as the Government collector of private indebtedness of officers/enlisted men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such matters should be litigated in civil courts. Where conduct may amount to conduct unbecoming, War Department may take action on those questions. (P. 64, 63, Feb. 1894; C. 5482, Dec. 1898.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mandatory statutory terms for details and return to duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory requirements (e.g., section 26 of Feb. 2, 1901) making details for fixed periods (four years) are mandatory: details terminate at expiration, and the Secretary may reassign the officer to duties conducive to public interest and may require new bonds if necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Held details must terminate at statutory period but Secretary may assign new duties and require new bond; C. 15844, Apr. 16, 1910.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope and limits on employment of Army to aid civil authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules govern when the Army may be employed to aid civil authority (to protect state from invasion or domestic violence, riots, etc.), including preconditions and limits on such use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proclamation will precede use of Federal troops; troops will not be placed under State control; the President judges size of force and territory to occupy; Republican form of state government cannot be overthrown; Posse Comitatus prohibits certain uses (though Army may serve process). Includes special rules for Alaska, Indian Country, Philippines (scouts), and prohibition on policing forest reserves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Army to enforce neutrality and limits on cross-border action
rubrics_metrics.description: Army may be used to prevent hostile expeditions leaving or crossing U.S. borders, to prevent violations of peace due to firing from across border, and to seize contraband supplies—but there are limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Military expedition defined; commanders should turn information of hostile expeditions over to civil authorities; armed forces cannot pursue hostile expedition into foreign territory; seized contraband should be turned to Federal civil authorities (not state). Commanding general should inform foreign commanding generals and may defend against cross-border fire. (Various pages/citations.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commanding general relations to State authorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Commanding general should maintain friendly relations with the State in which he is serving and cannot support State authorities in execution of State laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance emphasizes comity and separation of federal military power from state law enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protections regarding interned prisoners
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain protections apply to interned prisoners; e.g., their fingerprints may not be taken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interned prisoners: 'Finger prints of, may not be taken.' (contextual ruling)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary's limitations on grants and franchises
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War is without authority, unaided by legislation, to grant franchises in navigable waters or elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 9323, Nov. 23, 1900. Legislative authorization required to grant franchises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptance of conditional conveyances and binding the Government
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary cannot accept conditional conveyances that bind the Government by future conditions or create unliquidated claims against the United States absent statutory authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: deeds offered with conditions subsequent or provisos creating future claims could not legally be accepted. (P. 56, 263, Nov. 1892.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to sell used public property
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War has power to sell public property that has been used, and may fix the sale price of property which has been in use and repaired.

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority to loan Government property to other departments or outsiders
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no legal authority for the loan, by the Secretary of War, of Government property to other executive departments or to parties not in the Government service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary may withhold information from Court of Claims when prejudicial
rubrics_metrics.description: Under section 1076, R.S., the Secretary (or other department head) may refuse or omit to comply with a call of the Court of Claims for information or papers when he considers it prejudicial to the public interest; statute makes him sole judge on the subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: withholding a particular affidavit due to peculiar nature/immateriality. (P. 26, 497, Sept. 1888.)

rubrics_metrics.name: War Department limits on furnishing records to other executive departments
rubrics_metrics.description: When facts are to be ascertained for executive purposes, the War Department will answer proper inquiries as to the fact from its own records but will not furnish copies of records or statements to permit other executive branch members to review military decisions or make independent military decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice adopted to avoid confusion and waste; referenced circular of Nov. 2, 1901 and C. 10306, July 8, 1910.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary cannot abridge statutory appointments for general officers' aids
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary of War cannot lawfully limit the number of aides allowed to general officers where the number and appointment are granted by statute; executive regulation cannot abridge statutory grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public printing and need standard for departmental publications
rubrics_metrics.description: The Secretary may only cause publication by the Public Printer if the work is 'necessary' to administer the public business; 'necessary' construed as reasonably necessary or clearly conducive to the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Manual of Calisthenics cannot be authorized unless reasonably necessary; Commissary's Handbook and similar works needed in department business may be printed at Government Printing Office and paid from department allotment. (P.50, 444; C. 1679; C.18579.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Acting Secretary succession and delegation during absence/illness
rubrics_metrics.description: During illness or temporary absence of the Secretary, the Assistant Secretary must serve as Acting Secretary, unless the President directs otherwise; President may devolve duties upon heads of other departments or certain officers as directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Duties may be devolved on (a) head of other executive department, (b) any officer whose appointment is by President with Senate advice/consent, (c) commanding general of the Army, or (d) chief of any military bureau. Listed examples of officers included in classes (c) and (d). (C. 18175, Sept. 7, 1911.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualifications of attorneys appearing before War Department
rubrics_metrics.description: No special War Department regulations covering qualifications of attorneys; in practice any attorney with legal authority to represent a client in a particular matter will be heard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employment of counsel for public matters falls to Attorney General
rubrics_metrics.description: By statute (act of June 22, 1870), employment of counsel in cases of a public nature and settlement of their compensation is transferred to the Attorney General; heads of departments shall call upon Department of Justice for counsel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Section 189, R.S., and sections 356–367 R.S. Secretary will refer papers to Attorney General if he deems defense at Government expense just and expedient. (Citations: R. 37, 99; P. 50, 363; others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Circumstances for Government-provided counsel and relief
rubrics_metrics.description: When an officer acted in due performance of military duty and is sued or prosecuted, the Secretary may request the Attorney General to provide counsel and may favor congressional relief in appropriate cases where judgment resulted from official acts performed in good faith.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Numerous factual examples where counsel was requested/provided or relief recommended (constructing quartermaster dispute, removal of trespassing animals, travel-related suits, etc.). See cited cases and practice notes (multiple C. and P. citations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reopening settlements barred when payment accepted (statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Act of July 31, 1894 provides that any person accepting payment under a settlement by an auditor is precluded from obtaining a revision of such settlement as to items upon which payment is accepted; accounting officers have no jurisdiction to reopen such items upon newly discovered evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: VII Comp. Dec. 537; cited practice references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bonding obligations during staff assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of a department detailed to the General Staff remains under his original bond; while no obligation may accrue under the bond while so serving, the bonding company may be advised to remit premiums during such incumbency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 4396, Feb. 19, 1900 (example regarding Subsistence Department officer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of pay cannot be diverted without statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: When pay is forfeited as part of sentence, in the absence of specific statutory authority the forfeited pay cannot be diverted from the General Treasury to a departmental fund to make good an embezzled amount.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: soldier's forfeited pay could not be added to Subsistence Department appropriation to make good embezzlement loss. R. 43, 85, Nov. 1879.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation to Chief of Engineers for temporary property transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Secretary may legally delegate to the Chief of Engineers authority to direct temporary transfer of property purchased from one appropriation for use in another improvement, subject to equitable adjustment of charges and credits agreed by district officers under direction of Chief of Engineers.
